title: AI-Assisted Devices in University Written Examinations: A Structural Threat to the Degree as a Warrant of Competence
content: This paper examines a threat to academic integrity: undetectable cheating with contemporary technology in invigilated written university examinations. The threat is a cheating pipeline formed by the convergence of miniaturised cameras and earbuds, AI smart glasses with heads-up displays, and large language models that answer university-level questions to a passing standard. If used, this pipeline can compromise closed-book examinations. Once covert assistance is feasible, the format can no longer reliably distinguish a candidate's own work from a machine's, and so cannot substantiate the competence a degree certifies. This is a structural problem: it concerns what the examination can certify for the whole cohort, not only those who cheat. Drawing on a narrative review of the academic-integrity literature (1966-2025), UK Ofqual malpractice statistics (2019-2025), and a scan of commercially available AI-assisted devices (2026), it shows that device use in examinations is established and rising in secondary education, and that the conditions driving it plausibly extend to higher education, though sector-level evidence remains limited. It argues that examination design and certification must be reconsidered as an institutional responsibility, and that what a degree certifies in the age of ambient AI cannot be left to detection technology to settle.
